page.text:
The primary connective of mathematical deduction is the *conditional* or
*material implication*, denoted $P \Rightarrow Q$ and read *if $P$, then
$Q$*. Virtually every mathematical theorem is cast in this mold: given a
collection of hypotheses $P$, we establish that a conclusion $Q$
necessarily follows.

In colloquial speech, saying 'if it rains, I will bring an umbrella'
suggests a causal or temporal link. In mathematical logic, however, the
conditional is purely *truth-functional*: its truth value depends solely
on the truth values of $P$ and $Q$, free of any requirement of
psychological or causal connection. The conditional $P \Rightarrow Q$
makes a very precise claim: it is violated if and only if the hypothesis
$P$ is true while the conclusion $Q$ is false.

Consequently, whenever the antecedent $P$ is false, the conditional
$P \Rightarrow Q$ is automatically regarded as true. This convention is
known as *vacuous truth*. If a mathematician promises, 'Every element of
the empty set is an even integer,' the assertion is true because there
are no counterexamples—the premise that an element belongs to the empty
set is unconditionally false. Vacuous truth is not an arbitrary quirk of
formalization; it is essential for mathematical consistency, guaranteeing
that general laws apply uniformly to boundary cases without requiring
countless ad hoc exceptions.
